paragraphs: This paper studies how people acting together can influence a digital platform through the data its machine learning system uses. The authors model a collective that pools participants’ data and coordinates changes to their own contributions. The central question is how much influence such a group can achieve relative to its size.

The analysis covers three learning settings: nonparametric optimal learning, parametric risk minimization, and gradient-based optimization. For each setting, the authors develop coordinated strategies and describe success criteria as a function of collective size. This connects the organization of participants with properties of the platform’s learning procedure.

The authors also test their ideas on skill classification using tens of thousands of freelancer resumes. Across more than two thousand training runs of a BERT-like model, observed behavior closely corresponds to theoretical predictions. Together, these results support the possibility that collectives representing a very small fraction of participants can substantially influence a platform’s learning algorithm. The conclusion concerns the studied strategies and settings, rather than guaranteeing influence for every collective.
icml-2023-algorithmic-collective-action-.tldr: Coordinated changes to participants’ data can give even very small collectives substantial influence over a platform’s learning algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational cost of training graph neural networks for semi-supervised node classification. In this task, a model learns to classify graph nodes using a limited supply of labels. The authors argue that the usual end-to-end training process can be understood as a two-level optimization problem, and that solving it this way often consumes substantial computation and memory.

They introduce a different optimization framework based on a multi-view learning perspective. Its structure allows the learning problem to be handled through alternating optimization: different parts of the problem are updated in turn. The contribution therefore concerns how graph learning is organized and optimized, with efficiency as a central objective.

Extensive experiments show comparable or better predictive performance than the state-of-the-art baselines considered, together with substantially improved computation and memory efficiency. These findings suggest that changing the optimization framework can preserve strong node classification performance while reducing training demands. The reported advantage combines predictive quality and resource use, rather than relying on efficiency alone.
icml-2023-alternately-optimized-graph-ne.tldr: An alternating optimization framework makes semi-supervised graph learning more efficient while matching or improving the tested baselines’ predictive performance.

paragraphs: The paper seeks generative models that combine useful modeling flexibility with mathematical guarantees. Deep image generators can suffer from memorization or mode collapse, while classical methods often need restrictive assumptions about the entire data distribution. The authors partially bridge this gap by imposing structure on conditional distributions instead.

Their conditionally strongly log-concave models express a distribution as a product of conditional probability distributions, each satisfying strong log-concavity. Orthogonal projectors adapted to the data produce this factorization. This permits efficient parameter estimation and sampling with theoretical guarantees even when the full distribution is not globally log-concave. The key is that the required regularity holds within the conditional pieces.

Using wavelet packet projectors, the authors show conditional log-concavity for several challenging multiscale processes. Numerical demonstrations include the phi-four physical model and weak lensing convergence maps, at higher resolutions than previous work. These results illustrate how conditional structure can make scientifically relevant distributions accessible to principled generative modeling without requiring global log-concavity.
icml-2023-conditionally-strongly-log-con.tldr: Factoring distributions into strongly log-concave conditional pieces enables generative modeling with guarantees beyond globally log-concave distributions.

paragraphs: This paper equips graph neural networks with prediction sets that express uncertainty about a node’s label. Instead of returning only one answer, the procedure returns a collection of possible labels with a distribution-free guarantee of containing the true label at an arbitrarily high probability level. It operates as post-processing around an existing, potentially pretrained GNN.

The main idea is to spread node-level conformity scores through the graph so that uncertainty estimates incorporate neighboring information. The method uses network homophily, the tendency for connected nodes to be similar. It can also produce meaningful sets when the underlying model supplies only its top predicted class, broadening the kinds of GNN outputs it can use.

The empirical evaluation finds comparable or smaller average prediction sets and a substantially improved rate of correct singleton sets. Smaller sets make uncertainty statements more specific, while correct singleton sets give an unambiguous answer. The authors also study theoretical conditions under which smoothing improves set efficiency, so that particular improvement is conditional rather than universal.
icml-2023-conformal-prediction-sets-for-.tldr: Diffusing conformity scores across a graph gives GNNs prediction sets with coverage guarantees and improved empirical usefulness.

paragraphs: A ReLU layer can discard information by setting negative activations to zero. This paper asks when the layer nevertheless preserves enough information to distinguish every input within a bounded region. The property being studied is injectivity: two different permitted inputs must produce different outputs. The authors consider a closed ball and its non-negative portion.

The analysis combines frame theory with convex geometry, emphasizing how the ball’s radius interacts with the layer’s bias vector. This matters because invertibility is examined over a specified input region, so the size of that region and the biases jointly affect which information survives. Under restrictions expressed through an upper bound on the bias vector, the authors obtain a computationally feasible injectivity check.

The paper also provides explicit reconstruction formulas inspired by duality in frame theory. These connect the question of whether reconstruction is possible with a concrete way to carry it out. The resulting framework offers a route to quantifying invertibility and reconstructing inputs on the ball when the relevant injectivity conditions hold.
icml-2023-convex-geometry-of-relu-layers.tldr: Frame theory and convex geometry provide conditional injectivity checks and explicit input reconstruction formulas for ReLU layers on bounded regions.

paragraphs: This paper addresses poor generated samples in variational autoencoders by focusing on holes in the prior. The issue concerns how the distribution used to draw latent samples relates to the data distribution. The authors propose the Coupled Variational Autoencoder, which treats that relationship as an optimal transport problem.

Optimal transport provides a way to formulate a coupling between two distributions. C-VAE explicitly enforces such a coupling between the prior and the data, giving greater freedom in choosing the prior and providing a natural resolution of the prior-hole problem. Its use of entropic optimal transport also offers several optimization routes through primal, dual, and semi-dual formulations.

Experiments on synthetic and real data compare C-VAE with VAE, WAE, and InfoVAE alternatives. The reported improvements cover fidelity to the data, latent representation quality, and generated sample quality. These findings suggest that explicitly organizing the relationship between the prior and data can benefit both generation and representation learning in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-coupled-variational-autoencode.tldr: C-VAE uses optimal transport to couple prior and data distributions, improving latent representations and generated samples in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Message passing neural networks can struggle when a prediction depends on distant parts of a graph. Local communication can force too much information through restricted routes, a problem called over-squashing. Adding connections can help, but letting distant nodes communicate immediately at every layer can weaken the useful distinction between nearby and faraway nodes.

DRew changes the communication structure gradually. Its rewiring depends on the network layer, progressively making the graph more connected as processing proceeds. A separate delay mechanism permits skip connections according to both the layer and the distance between nodes. Together, these mechanisms make distance relevant to how information travels through the model.

The framework is designed to apply to any message passing neural network architecture. On several tasks requiring long-range interactions, the authors report better performance than graph Transformers and multi-hop message passing networks. The findings support gradual rewiring and distance-dependent delays as useful ways to improve long-range communication while retaining information about the original graph’s distances.
icml-2023-drew-dynamically-rewired-messa.tldr: DRew improves long-range graph learning through gradual rewiring and communication delays that depend on graph distance.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous treatment effect estimation asks how a treatment’s effect varies across individuals or circumstances. Observational data make this difficult because treatment selection can depend on people’s characteristics, and outcomes under treatments they did not receive are unavailable. The authors focus on describing this selection bias in a way that extends beyond two treatment choices.

They use mutual information between observed covariates and treatments to characterize selection bias. From this quantity, they derive an error bound covering general treatment schemes, including multiple discrete options and continuous treatments. This gives a common theoretical framework for settings that existing selection-bias approaches do not naturally accommodate.

The resulting Mutual Information Treatment Network, or MitNet, uses adversarial optimization to reduce selection bias and improve treatment effect estimates. Its design is supported by the paper’s theoretical analysis. The authors report strong performance in simulation and empirical evaluation. The contribution therefore links a broader mathematical description of treatment assignment with a learning procedure intended to make that description useful in estimation.
icml-2023-estimating-heterogeneous-treat.tldr: Mutual information yields treatment-effect error bounds for general treatment spaces and motivates MitNet’s adversarial approach to reducing selection bias.

paragraphs: Learning a PDE solution operator means learning a mapping from input functions to the corresponding solutions. Practical problems complicate this task through irregular meshes, multiple input functions, and solution behavior spanning different scales. GNOT is a Transformer-based framework designed to address these difficulties within one operator-learning model.

The architecture introduces a heterogeneous normalized attention layer that accommodates different input functions and irregular spatial discretizations. It also uses geometric gating, which the authors interpret as a soft decomposition of the domain. This provides a mechanism for handling multiscale problems by organizing processing according to geometry without requiring a hard division into separate regions.

Experiments across challenging datasets from different domains show substantial improvements over the alternative methods evaluated. The authors also identify the Transformer’s large capacity as offering the possibility of scaling to larger datasets and practical applications. That scaling potential complements the demonstrated results: the empirical evidence establishes improvements on the studied problems, while the architecture supplies a flexible basis for broader use.
icml-2023-gnot-a-general-neural-operator.tldr: GNOT combines flexible attention and geometric gating to learn PDE solution operators with irregular meshes, multiple inputs, and multiscale behavior.

paragraphs: Many graph neural networks assume every node is described by the same fixed set of features. Real graphs can violate both parts of that assumption: nodes may have different features, and features may appear or disappear over time. GRAFENNE addresses these changing inputs without relying on a fixed feature inventory.

The framework transforms the graph using a bipartite encoding that separates nodes from features. A specially chosen message passing procedure then makes the number of model parameters independent of the feature count. This enables the model to handle previously unseen nodes and previously unseen features, extending its ability to generalize beyond the original graph representation.

The authors prove that GRAFENNE is at least as expressive as existing message passing GNNs under the Weisfeiler-Leman test framework. Thus, its additional feature flexibility does not reduce expressivity in that formal comparison. Experiments on four real-world graphs also demonstrate strong empirical performance and continual learning over streaming feature sets, connecting the representation change to practical handling of evolving graph data.
icml-2023-grafenne-learning-on-graphs-wi.tldr: GRAFENNE separates nodes and features to handle unseen and changing features while preserving message passing expressivity.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimating an unknown translation of a known probability distribution from a finite sample. Classical maximum likelihood theory describes optimal asymptotic accuracy using Fisher information and the Cramér-Rao bound. However, the sample size needed for that approximation can depend strongly on the distribution and can be arbitrarily large.

The authors develop finite-sample error bounds using smoothed estimators. Their guarantees depend on the Fisher information of a smoothed version of the distribution. As the sample size grows, the smoothing amount decreases at an explicit rate, and the bound approaches the classical Cramér-Rao limit. This connects a finite-data guarantee with the familiar asymptotic benchmark.

The work improves one-dimensional results to include convergence at constant failure probability as well as high probability, and extends the theory to high-dimensional distributions. Along the way, it proves a new concentration bound for the norm of a random vector whose one-dimensional projections are subgamma. That auxiliary result controls the vector’s overall magnitude and may be useful beyond location estimation.
icml-2023-high-dimensional-location-esti.tldr: Smoothed estimators provide finite-sample location-estimation bounds that extend to high dimensions and approach the Cramér-Rao limit.

paragraphs: A learnware market stores trained models together with specifications describing what they can do. Users can search these descriptions to find reusable models, while developers can contribute models without disclosing their training data. This paper addresses a difficult case: none of the available models has exactly the label space needed by the user.

The authors improve specifications based on Reduced Kernel Mean Embedding by explicitly describing models at the class level. They pair these class-specific descriptions with a class-wise identification method. This makes the search sensitive to relevant individual classes, allowing useful models to be identified even when their overall labeling tasks differ from the requested one.

Theoretical and empirical analyses support fast, accurate identification of models meeting user requirements. The authors also find that, for a specific task, a small model selected through its specification performs better than directly reusing a generic pretrained large model. This result highlights the value of matching a model’s capabilities to the task, rather than treating model size as sufficient evidence of usefulness.
icml-2023-identifying-useful-learnwares-.tldr: Class-specific model descriptions help users find reusable models even when available models have different label spaces.

paragraphs: This paper develops an understandable neural network whose prediction score is a sum of separate spline functions, each acting on one input variable. The additive structure makes the contribution associated with each variable explicit. The proposed network extends existing approaches built around additive models, splines, and neural additive models.

The authors show that this network can be approximated by logistic regression applied to nonlinearly transformed inputs. Initially, the transformation depends on the neural network’s random initialization. They then establish that a deterministic kernel-based transformation can replace it, removing that dependence on the initial random network.

This replacement leads to guaranteed convergence of training and a unique solution for a given training dataset in the resulting formulation. The contribution connects an interpretable nonlinear score with a training problem whose outcome is mathematically well determined. The approximation statement is central: the paper links the proposed network to kernel logistic regression, rather than claiming that every ReLU network admits the same interpretable structure or training guarantee.
icml-2023-kernel-logistic-regression-app.tldr: An additive spline neural network admits a kernel logistic regression approximation with deterministic preprocessing and guaranteed training convergence.

paragraphs: Scientific machine learning models increasingly incorporate partial differential equations, but difficult equation classes can require particularly careful enforcement of conservation constraints. The paper focuses on this issue, including cases where controlling a conserved volume is essential. ProbConserv is proposed as a framework for adding such constraints to a generic scientific learning architecture.

The method combines an integral expression of a conservation law with a Bayesian update. This connects physical consistency with probabilistic prediction, allowing the framework to enforce conservation while retaining uncertainty quantification. The authors analyze it using the Generalized Porous Medium Equation, a parameterized family that exhibits both easier and harder PDE behavior.

On easier variants, ProbConserv performs well alongside state-of-the-art competitors. On harder variants, it outperforms approaches that do not guarantee volume conservation. The reported results also show effective handling of shocks and varying uncertainty across observations, together with superior downstream predictive performance in the studied cases. These findings make conservation enforcement part of the model’s predictive behavior, rather than merely an additional descriptive requirement.
icml-2023-learning-physical-models-that-.tldr: ProbConserv combines conservation laws with Bayesian updates to enforce physical constraints while preserving uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: This paper asks how offline demonstrations can improve an agent’s later online learning, and how that benefit depends on demonstration quality. The authors study Thompson sampling in a multi-armed bandit, where a learner repeatedly chooses among actions with uncertain rewards. They introduce a notion of expert competence to describe the source of the demonstrations.

Their informed Thompson sampling algorithm incorporates the demonstrations through Bayes’ rule. This provides a coherent way to let prior observations shape online decisions. A prior-dependent Bayesian regret bound relates the method’s performance to the information available before online learning and gives insight into why more competent experts can produce greater improvement.

The authors also develop a practical approximation using Bayesian bootstrapping. Experiments show substantial reductions in regret, meaning less reward is lost through imperfect action choices. The theoretical and empirical contributions together explain why demonstrations should be evaluated by their quality as well as their availability, with the formal analysis grounded in the stated bandit and expert-competence model.
icml-2023-leveraging-demonstrations-to-i.tldr: An informed Thompson sampling method uses demonstrations through Bayesian updating, with benefits that increase with expert competence.

paragraphs: LongCoder addresses code completion when the available code context is long. Useful information can occur far from the point being completed, including earlier imports and definitions. The paper introduces a task focused on this setting and proposes a sparse Transformer designed to combine local processing with access to distant information.

Its attention mechanism uses a sliding window alongside two kinds of globally accessible tokens. Bridge tokens are distributed through the input to collect local information and support interaction across the sequence. Memory tokens highlight statements likely to matter later, such as imports and definitions of classes, functions, or structures. The two mechanisms give global communication and explicit retention of important code distinct roles.

The authors evaluate LongCoder on a newly constructed dataset with longer code contexts and on CodeXGLUE. It outperforms previous models on the tested completion tasks while using comparable computational resources during inference. The result supports the usefulness of selective global access for long-context completion without a corresponding increase in reported inference resource demands.
icml-2023-longcoder-a-long-range-pre-tra.tldr: LongCoder combines local attention with bridge and memory tokens to improve long-context code completion at comparable inference cost.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning can benefit when related tasks share useful knowledge, but sharing can also cause interference. A fixed, manually designed architecture decides in advance where that sharing occurs. This paper proposes Multi-Task Structural Learning, or MTSL, which learns the architecture together with its parameters as training proceeds.

MTSL starts with a separate network of the same design for each task. It alternates between task learning, where each network specializes, and structural learning, where locally similar task layers are grouped. Beginning at early layers, those layers transfer knowledge into a newly created shared group layer. The original layers are then removed and replaced by that group layer before the procedure considers subsequent layers.

This process makes sharing depend on similarities found during learning. The reported experiments show generalization competitive with several baselines and improved robustness on out-of-distribution data. The findings support adapting the network’s structure as a way to manage task relationships, while the generalization result is competitive rather than a claim of uniformly superior accuracy.
icml-2023-multi-task-structural-learning.tldr: MTSL learns which task layers to share during training, achieving competitive generalization and improved out-of-distribution robustness.

paragraphs: This paper reexamines whether visual pretraining delivers clear advantages for control tasks that use images to guide actions. The authors revisit a simple learning-from-scratch approach using a shallow convolutional network and data augmentation. They compare it with PVR, MVP, and R3M approaches that use frozen visual representations pretrained on large vision datasets.

The simple baseline is surprisingly competitive across multiple learning algorithms, task domains, and evaluation measures, both in simulation and on a real robot. This makes the baseline consequential for evaluating progress: comparisons need to account for what a straightforward task-trained visual model can already achieve.

The authors attribute a substantial obstacle for the pretrained methods to the domain gap between their pretraining data and the visual control benchmarks. Fine-tuning alleviates that mismatch. The findings therefore concern how pretrained representations transfer and whether they remain frozen, rather than establishing that pretraining is generally unhelpful. The paper uses this evidence to offer recommendations for future pretraining research and stronger benchmarking.
icml-2023-on-pre-training-for-visuo-moto.tldr: A shallow vision model trained from scratch competes strongly with frozen pretrained representations, whose domain mismatch is alleviated by fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using information from a teacher model. This paper investigates whether its benefits extend beyond predictive accuracy to interpretability. The authors quantify one aspect of interpretability through network dissection, counting internal concept detectors identified in the model.

Their proposed explanation centers on class-similarity information transferred from teacher to student. They first confirm that logit distillation conveys this information, then examine how interpretability changes with its presence, absence, and degree. This connects the observed interpretability benefit to what the teacher communicates about relationships among classes.

The study includes quantitative and qualitative experiments across datasets, distillation methods, and interpretability measures. Its results support the claim that distillation can improve both accuracy and interpretability in the evaluated models. The practical implication is that a teacher’s guidance may shape how a student represents concepts, as well as how accurately it predicts. The evidence grounds interpretability in the measures examined, including identifiable concept detectors within the network.
icml-2023-on-the-impact-of-knowledge-dis.tldr: The study links improved student-model interpretability under knowledge distillation to class-similarity information transferred by the teacher.

paragraphs: Calibration concerns whether predicted probabilities agree with how often outcomes occur. This paper introduces Online Platt Scaling, or OPS, to adjust a model’s outputs as observations arrive. It combines Platt scaling with online logistic regression, making post-processing responsive to incoming data rather than relying entirely on one fixed calibration fit.

The authors demonstrate that OPS adapts between independent, identically distributed data and settings with distribution drift. They also address a further problem: even the best available Platt scaling model may remain miscalibrated. Adding a technique called calibeating makes the procedure more robust to that situation, and the combined method has a calibration guarantee for adversarial outcome sequences.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, both with and without drift, show superior performance without hyperparameter tuning. The authors also extend the approach to beta scaling. Together, the contributions provide an adaptive calibration procedure, a theoretical guarantee for its strengthened version, and evidence that the approach works across several evaluated data conditions.
icml-2023-online-platt-scaling-with-cali.tldr: Online Platt Scaling adapts probability calibration to incoming data, while calibeating adds a guarantee for adversarial outcome sequences.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe changes to an input that would produce a different prediction. Their usefulness can depend on whether they remain valid after the model changes. This paper questions measuring such changes only through parameter distance, since parameters can shift substantially while predictions on the data remain almost unchanged.

The authors define naturally-occurring model change by limiting prediction changes on the data manifold while allowing arbitrary parameter changes. They introduce a Stability measure for counterfactuals in differentiable models. Using concentration bounds for Lipschitz functions of independent Gaussian variables, they show that sufficiently high Stability gives a high-probability guarantee of validity after changes covered by their framework.

The measure depends on a local Lipschitz constant, which may not be available in practice. The authors therefore examine practical relaxations and experimentally incorporate them into counterfactual search. The resulting explanations are reported to be close, realistic, and resilient to potential model changes. The theoretical guarantee remains tied to sufficiently high Stability and the specified model-change framework.
icml-2023-robust-counterfactual-explanat.tldr: A Stability measure gives probabilistic robustness guarantees for counterfactual explanations under a prediction-based model of model change.

paragraphs: This paper studies how agents can learn useful strategies for learning from others. The authors use deep reinforcement learning to optimize social learning in a cooperative game over a multidimensional landscape. Training aims to maximize overall payoff, allowing the learning process to search for effective social behavior.

Without explicit instruction in social learning concepts, the agent develops behaviors including copying, attending to frequent and successful neighbors, and comparing others with itself. It also learns long-term cooperation and the importance of balancing individual exploration with learning socially. These behaviors emerge from optimizing the game objective rather than being supplied as predefined strategies.

The fully trained agent achieves higher mean payoff than all traditional baseline social learning strategies considered. Further evaluations include changing environments and real social networks, supporting the framework’s adaptability across the tested social settings. The study demonstrates how reward-driven training can generate recognizable social learning heuristics and combine them effectively, offering a computational approach to questions about when and how learning from others is advantageous.
icml-2023-social-learning-spontaneously-.tldr: Reinforcement learning produces social learning strategies without explicit guidance and outperforms the traditional strategies tested.

paragraphs: Artificial neural networks are often evaluated as models of brain systems by comparing their responses with biological recordings. A good match is then treated as evidence supporting the model. This paper asks how much those comparisons actually reveal about the underlying computational architecture.

The authors replace biological recordings with responses from models whose architecture is already known. This creates a setting where a comparison method’s identification can be checked against ground truth. They evaluate commonly used techniques, including linear encoding models and centered kernel alignment, to determine whether these methods correctly identify the model responsible for the responses.

Identification performance varies substantially and depends on factors separate from the true architecture, including the stimulus images used. The authors also show limitations in using functional similarity scores to recover higher-level architectural motifs. The findings indicate that reproducing responses and identifying architectural structure are distinct achievements. Consequently, a strong similarity score needs careful interpretation when used as evidence about how a neural system computes.
icml-2023-system-identification-of-neura.tldr: Tests with known models show that neural-response similarity methods can be unreliable guides to underlying architecture.

paragraphs: Graph clustering aims to separate vertices into meaningful groups. Some graph neural networks learn these groups using a relaxed minimum-cut objective based on spectral clustering. This paper argues that the relaxation is loose and can produce excessively smooth assignments, weakening the separation between clusters.

The authors instead use a tighter relaxation based on graph total variation. Their model combines a message passing layer that minimizes the absolute, or L1, differences between neighboring vertex features with an unsupervised loss on cluster assignments. The loss minimizes graph total variation while encouraging balanced partitions. This formulation is designed to support sharper transitions between clusters.

The learned assignments can directly define vertex clusters or serve as graph pooling within a graph classification system. Experiments show better performance than the other GNNs evaluated on both vertex clustering and graph classification. The results connect the choice of optimization objective to the usefulness of the learned groups: sharper, balanced assignments can support both local grouping and downstream prediction about an entire graph.
icml-2023-total-variation-graph-neural-n.tldr: A graph total variation objective produces sharper cluster assignments and improves the reported clustering and graph classification results.

paragraphs: Long-tailed visual recognition involves classes with very different amounts of training data. Sparse observations, noise, and differences between training and testing distributions make this setting challenging. The paper proposes Wrapped Cauchy Distributed Angular Softmax, or WCDAS, to improve how a classifier models class information in its output function.

WCDAS incorporates sample-specific Gaussian-based kernels into the angular relationship between feature representations and classifier weights. Each class’s angular distribution becomes a mixture of these kernels. The theoretical analysis supports a wrapped Cauchy distribution over a Gaussian distribution for approximating the mixed distributions considered. Trainable concentration parameters also adjust each class’s compactness and margin dynamically.

Empirical results show that these concentration parameters behave in a label-aware way. Across multiple long-tailed visual recognition benchmarks, WCDAS outperforms the state-of-the-art softmax-based alternatives evaluated. The contribution combines a distributional model of angular features with class-specific adaptation, addressing the uneven and noisy evidence available across classes within the classifier’s scoring mechanism.
icml-2023-wrapped-cauchy-distributed-ang.tldr: WCDAS models angular class distributions with adaptive concentration parameters to improve visual recognition on long-tailed datasets.
